topic: University co-op placements and career pathways

turns.text: Dan, how did you get here to NASA?
I was poor and I needed money. I was in college, and my roommate and I decided we should probably try to make some money, so we figured let's go get internships.

My school had a well set-up co-op program. I was immediately presented with a list of companies, and NASA was on the list. I was a business major and went to school with nothing but engineers, so I wondered what I could do there.
They told you NASA had business functions too, such as budget and contracts.
I interviewed and got the position. I spent a semester in a budget office, but it was not for me. The co-op program let me come back for multiple tours and try something else.

I liked writing and talking, so I tried public affairs, passed a writing test, and spent a summer there. The shuttle mission that repaired Hubble got me hooked. I kept coming back, and NASA offered me a job by the time I graduated.
That's one good thing about the co-op program: if you keep coming back, your chances are good.
Chances are good that you might be here at NASA.
He's got to weigh them down a little bit; it's all right.

keyPoints: Dan and his roommate sought internships while he was a college business major
The university co-op program showed Dan employer options including NASA
Dan worried NASA was only for engineers but learned it also had business roles
A budget-office semester was a poor fit, so the co-op let Dan try public affairs
Dan's public affairs placement and Hubble mission experience drew him into NASA work
